At each placement Wang's sampling puts some of the remaining stones on offer (all of them once only a few are left), and you choose which candidate to place: a stone on offer in one of four rotations, at the position Wang's image convolution found for it. Every listed candidate is feasible (LLC > 0). Your goal is the finished wall, judged on four metrics: F_SF, stone filling (the share of the wall area that is stone, higher is better); F_AH, the horizontal joint path index (lower is better: no long continuous horizontal joints); F_AV, the vertical joint path index (higher is better: vertical joints are staggered); F_LR, the smaller of the left and right kinematic limit loads of the wall divided by the friction coefficient (higher is better). All four metrics must be good: F_SF, F_AH, F_AV and F_LR. Do not sacrifice the others for one of them. A stone that cannot be placed is lost to the wall.
Data. Stones are labelled S1, S2, ... in the order they were first sampled. Coordinates are pixels in the evaluation frame (mirrored when building from the right, so 'left' is the side the course is built from); rows count upward from the ground. Each candidate: id, stone, rotation, its pose x and y, the width and height of its bounding box, and Wang's five filter scores (higher is better for each): NHR course height (0 = level with its left neighbour), GDS global density, IWR interlocking (its vertical joint far from the joints below), LLC the kinematic limit load of the wall with the stone added and stabilized, divided by the friction coefficient, LFR local void (0 = flush on the left and on the bottom). n_remaining counts the stones not yet placed, on offer or not; wall summarizes the current wall; unplaceable lists stones on offer with no feasible candidate now. Nothing about the final wall is known.
Before committing you may call check_after with one or more candidate ids (comma-separated). For each, it returns how many feasible poses (0 to 4, at most one per rotation) every other stone on offer now would have at the very next placement if that candidate were placed now. 0 means that stone could not be placed next; the counts can change again after later placements. While more stones remain than are on offer, the next placement's offer is a new sample, so a stone on offer now may not be on offer next. It gives no scores.
Compare the main candidates on all five scores and on what they leave for the remaining stones; in the rationale state each one's main advantages and costs. Finish with commit_pick.
Lessons. The advice below was written after studying finished walls, good and bad, built with this method from other sets of stones. It is advice, not rules: weigh it against what this placement shows.
1. Protect future placements first. Use check_after on promising candidates, especially when choices are narrowing or offered stones are unplaceable. Compare how many other offered stones retain poses, avoid newly blocking them, and value reopening blocked stones. This is only a one-step, on-offer check, not a guarantee of eventual placement.
2. When a feasible offered stone has few candidate rotations, consider placing it before its opportunity disappears, provided check_after does not reveal worse consequences for the others. A currently unplaceable stone is not necessarily lost: another placement may make it feasible again.
3. Favor high LLC relative to the available alternatives, particularly early in construction; avoid a large drop merely to win another filter. Treat LLC as a useful stability signal, not a guarantee of the finished wall’s load, and accept a compromise when needed to preserve placement options.
4. While forming early courses, favor well-fitting, reasonably level placements and, where alternatives are otherwise comparable, wider rather than tall narrow orientations. Avoid repeatedly building upward before the course is filled. NHR and bounding-box shape are clues, not reasons to enforce a perfectly flat skyline.
5. Balance interlocking with density and local fit: a candidate with the highest IWR can still be a poor choice if it gives up substantial LLC, GDS or LFR. Compare scores against the alternatives at that placement; even a GDS of zero can be tied for best when a new course starts.

arguments.rationale: S21 at 270° combines best LLC (0.517), GDS (1.0) and LFR (-0.050) with reasonable NHR (-0.581) and IWR (0.665). It leaves S1 three poses and S8 four. S21 at 0° is wider with the same LLC and GDS, but has worse NHR, IWR and LFR and leaves S1 only two poses. S8 at 90° has slightly better IWR (0.769) and also leaves seven poses across the others, but sacrifices LLC (0.345) and local fit. The scarce S1 has excellent IWR (4.449) and NHR (-0.221), and placing it leaves all eight other poses, but its LLC (0.172) and LFR (-0.180) are substantially worse. The wide S8 orientations retain top LLC but have zero GDS, poor NHR and weak IWR; S21 at 180° is similarly weak and leaves fewer options. These are one-step checks, not guarantees.

At each placement Wang's sampling puts some of the remaining stones on offer (all of them once only a few are left), and you choose which candidate to place: a stone on offer in one of four rotations, at the position Wang's image convolution found for it. Every listed candidate is feasible (LLC > 0). Your goal is the finished wall, judged on four metrics: F_SF, stone filling (the share of the wall area that is stone, higher is better); F_AH, the horizontal joint path index (lower is better: no long continuous horizontal joints); F_AV, the vertical joint path index (higher is better: vertical joints are staggered); F_LR, the smaller of the left and right kinematic limit loads of the wall divided by the friction coefficient (higher is better). All four metrics must be good: F_SF, F_AH, F_AV and F_LR. Do not sacrifice the others for one of them. A stone that cannot be placed is lost to the wall.
Data. Stones are labelled S1, S2, ... in the order they were first sampled. Coordinates are pixels in the evaluation frame (mirrored when building from the right, so 'left' is the side the course is built from); rows count upward from the ground. Each candidate: id, stone, rotation, its pose x and y, the width and height of its bounding box, and Wang's five filter scores (higher is better for each): NHR course height (0 = level with its left neighbour), GDS global density, IWR interlocking (its vertical joint far from the joints below), LLC the kinematic limit load of the wall with the stone added and stabilized, divided by the friction coefficient, LFR local void (0 = flush on the left and on the bottom). n_remaining counts the stones not yet placed, on offer or not; wall summarizes the current wall; unplaceable lists stones on offer with no feasible candidate now. Nothing about the final wall is known.
Before committing you may call check_after with one or more candidate ids (comma-separated). For each, it returns how many feasible poses (0 to 4, at most one per rotation) every other stone on offer now would have at the very next placement if that candidate were placed now. 0 means that stone could not be placed next; the counts can change again after later placements. While more stones remain than are on offer, the next placement's offer is a new sample, so a stone on offer now may not be on offer next. It gives no scores.
Compare the main candidates on all five scores and on what they leave for the remaining stones; in the rationale state each one's main advantages and costs. Finish with commit_pick.
Lessons. The advice below was written after studying finished walls, good and bad, built with this method from other sets of stones. It is advice, not rules: weigh it against what this placement shows.
1. Protect future placements first. Use check_after on promising candidates, especially when choices are narrowing or offered stones are unplaceable. Compare how many other offered stones retain poses, avoid newly blocking them, and value reopening blocked stones. This is only a one-step, on-offer check, not a guarantee of eventual placement.
2. When a feasible offered stone has few candidate rotations, consider placing it before its opportunity disappears, provided check_after does not reveal worse consequences for the others. A currently unplaceable stone is not necessarily lost: another placement may make it feasible again.
3. Favor high LLC relative to the available alternatives, particularly early in construction; avoid a large drop merely to win another filter. Treat LLC as a useful stability signal, not a guarantee of the finished wall’s load, and accept a compromise when needed to preserve placement options.
4. While forming early courses, favor well-fitting, reasonably level placements and, where alternatives are otherwise comparable, wider rather than tall narrow orientations. Avoid repeatedly building upward before the course is filled. NHR and bounding-box shape are clues, not reasons to enforce a perfectly flat skyline.
5. Balance interlocking with density and local fit: a candidate with the highest IWR can still be a poor choice if it gives up substantial LLC, GDS or LFR. Compare scores against the alternatives at that placement; even a GDS of zero can be tied for best when a new course starts.

arguments.rationale: S8 at 180° combines joint-best LLC 0.517 and GDS 1.0 with a wide, nearly level placement (NHR -0.054), good local fit (LFR -0.018) and IWR 0.500. S11 at 0° is comparably level and stable, but fits slightly less well and has slightly lower IWR; both leave the other offered stones with 4 and 3 poses. S8 at 0° leaves the same options but has worse NHR and LFR than 180°. S16 at 90° preserves four poses for each other stone, but gives up density, stability and fit; its 270° orientation matches LLC but has GDS 0 and worse NHR and LFR. S16 at 0° offers the highest IWR and preserves all eight other poses, but sacrifices substantial LLC and density. The tall S8 and S11 orientations likewise trade stability and fit for interlocking, especially at 270°. These one-step pose counts do not guarantee later placements; 6 offers the strongest balanced fit and stability without newly blocking either offered stone.

All four metrics must be good: F_SF, F_AH, F_AV and F_LR. Do not sacrifice the others for one of them. A stone that cannot be placed is lost to the wall.

payload.instructions:
You build a dry-stone wall from the first stone to the last. The wall is built course by course with Wang's method. At each placement Wang's sampling puts some of the remaining stones on offer (all of them once only a few are left), and you choose which candidate to place: a stone on offer in one of four rotations, at the position Wang's image convolution found for it. Every listed candidate is feasible (LLC > 0). Your goal is the finished wall, judged on four metrics: F_SF, stone filling (the share of the wall area that is stone, higher is better); F_AH, the horizontal joint path index (lower is better: no long continuous horizontal joints); F_AV, the vertical joint path index (higher is better: vertical joints are staggered); F_LR, the smaller of the left and right kinematic limit loads of the wall divided by the friction coefficient (higher is better). All four metrics must be good: F_SF, F_AH, F_AV and F_LR. Do not sacrifice the others for one of them. A stone that cannot be placed is lost to the wall.
Data. Stones are labelled S1, S2, ... in the order they were first sampled. Coordinates are pixels in the evaluation frame (mirrored when building from the right, so 'left' is the side the course is built from); rows count upward from the ground. Each candidate: id, stone, rotation, its pose x and y, the width and height of its bounding box, and Wang's five filter scores (higher is better for each): NHR course height (0 = level with its left neighbour), GDS global density, IWR interlocking (its vertical joint far from the joints below), LLC the kinematic limit load of the wall with the stone added and stabilized, divided by the friction coefficient, LFR local void (0 = flush on the left and on the bottom). n_remaining counts the stones not yet placed, on offer or not; wall summarizes the current wall; unplaceable lists stones on offer with no feasible candidate now. Nothing about the final wall is known.
Before committing you may call check_after with one or more candidate ids (comma-separated). For each, it returns how many feasible poses (0 to 4, at most one per rotation) every other stone on offer now would have at the very next placement if that candidate were placed now. 0 means that stone could not be placed next; the counts can change again after later placements. While more stones remain than are on offer, the next placement's offer is a new sample, so a stone on offer now may not be on offer next. It gives no scores.
Compare the main candidates on all five scores and on what they leave for the remaining stones; in the rationale state each one's main advantages and costs. Finish with commit_pick.
Lessons. The advice below was written after studying finished walls, good and bad, built with this method from other sets of stones. It is advice, not rules: weigh it against what this placement shows.
1. Protect future placements first. Use check_after on promising candidates, especially when choices are narrowing or offered stones are unplaceable. Compare how many other offered stones retain poses, avoid newly blocking them, and value reopening blocked stones. This is only a one-step, on-offer check, not a guarantee of eventual placement.
2. When a feasible offered stone has few candidate rotations, consider placing it before its opportunity disappears, provided check_after does not reveal worse consequences for the others. A currently unplaceable stone is not necessarily lost: another placement may make it feasible again.
3. Favor high LLC relative to the available alternatives, particularly early in construction; avoid a large drop merely to win another filter. Treat LLC as a useful stability signal, not a guarantee of the finished wall’s load, and accept a compromise when needed to preserve placement options.
4. While forming early courses, favor well-fitting, reasonably level placements and, where alternatives are otherwise comparable, wider rather than tall narrow orientations. Avoid repeatedly building upward before the course is filled. NHR and bounding-box shape are clues, not reasons to enforce a perfectly flat skyline.
5. Balance interlocking with density and local fit: a candidate with the highest IWR can still be a poor choice if it gives up substantial LLC, GDS or LFR. Compare scores against the alternatives at that placement; even a GDS of zero can be tied for best when a new course starts.

Balance interlocking with density and local fit: a candidate with the highest IWR can still be a poor choice if it gives up substantial LLC, GDS or LFR. Compare scores against the alternatives at that placement; even a GDS of zero can be tied for best when a new course starts.

Protect future placements first. Use check_after on promising candidates, especially when choices are narrowing or offered stones are unplaceable. Compare how many other offered stones retain poses, avoid newly blocking them, and value reopening blocked stones. This is only a one-step, on-offer check, not a guarantee of eventual placement.

When a feasible offered stone has few candidate rotations, consider placing it before its opportunity disappears, provided check_after does not reveal worse consequences for the others. A currently unplaceable stone is not necessarily lost: another placement may make it feasible again.

Favor high LLC relative to the available alternatives, particularly early in construction; avoid a large drop merely to win another filter. Treat LLC as a useful stability signal, not a guarantee of the finished wall’s load, and accept a compromise when needed to preserve placement options.
